title: Senior RAP testing, performance and production
intro: Defend the evidence behind a cloud service: observable behavior, failure recovery, real consumer security, measured performance and reliable delivery. All scenarios are hypothetical; no SAP execution is implied.

questions.question: How would you test a Submit action without replacing the business object you are supposed to verify?
questions.answer: Keep the Submit implementation and its relevant BO behavior real. Isolate true dependencies such as database tables, external service adapters or other BOs using the appropriate supported doubles. Drive the operation through a meaningful boundary, often EML, and assert state changes, failures and messages. A double of the very action under test would prove the configured double response rather than the business rule.
questions.detail: A purchase request can be submitted only when every item has an account assignment. Test a valid request and a missing assignment, including persisted outcome after the supported save boundary. If another BO supplies a limit, double that dependency and vary its response.
questions.pitfall: Do not label a test of a mocked Submit response as a test of Submit.
followups: Which behavior remains real?
How do you prove rejected data was not persisted?
questions.evidence: Show the dependency diagram and a failing test when the real Submit check is deliberately broken.

questions.question: When would SQL doubles, CDS doubles and RAP BO doubles give misleading confidence?
questions.answer: They isolate different dependencies. SQL doubles replace table access, CDS doubles support tests of CDS logic, and RAP BO doubles isolate dependent EML behavior. Choose the boundary according to the risk being tested. Generic BO buffer doubles do not execute arbitrary custom provider rules, and access-control behavior needs explicit treatment. Complement isolated tests with targeted integration tests for actual persistence, authorization and service contracts.
questions.detail: A calculation test may use a SQL double successfully while a dependent action contract changes unnoticed. Conversely, a mocked EML response can test consumer error handling without proving the provider action. Name exactly which conclusion each test supports.
questions.pitfall: A more sophisticated double does not automatically provide broader integration evidence.
followups: Does this double execute custom determinations?
Which real boundary still needs verification?
questions.evidence: Record test scope and verify one representative path through the real provider and service.

questions.question: A bulk EML action processes ten requests and rejects two. What should its test assert?
questions.answer: Assert each input-to-result correlation and the intended atomicity contract, not just the number of messages. Verify which identities appear in FAILED, where reported messages point, and what changes remain buffered or persisted after transaction completion. Cover failures during interaction and save separately. The desired all-or-nothing or permitted partial-result behavior must be explicit and supported by the chosen request boundary.
questions.detail: Use nonsequential keys and distinct invalid reasons so accidental row-position correlation is visible. Reorder input and response fixtures. Include a successful interaction followed by a save rejection, and ensure the consumer does not report that object as durably complete.
questions.pitfall: Do not equate ten returned messages with ten correct operation outcomes.
followups: Which failures occur only on save?
Can the caller correlate reordered results?
questions.evidence: Show expected accepted/rejected identities, field messages and final persisted rows for each failure phase.

questions.question: A draft test passes when run alone but fails after another test. What would you inspect?
questions.answer: Inspect shared fixtures, draft and active identities, transactional buffers, locks and double-environment lifecycle. Each test must establish its own relevant state and release/reset supported test resources. Do not use uncontrolled commits to make a suite pass. Verify draft-specific actions and the chosen test framework boundaries rather than assuming an active-instance fixture represents a draft.
questions.detail: Two tests reuse the same business key but differ in draft context. One leaves a buffer or configured double response behind. Run the pair in reversed order and with distinct fixtures, then fix lifecycle isolation while preserving the scenario being tested.
questions.pitfall: A test that depends on execution order is unreliable evidence for draft behavior.
followups: Are active and draft transactional keys distinct?
Which setup/teardown resource is shared?
questions.evidence: Run the isolated tests, both orders and the suite; retain evidence of deterministic results.

questions.question: How do you prove optimistic concurrency rather than merely calling the same update twice?
questions.answer: Use independent consumers or sessions that read the same initial version, then perform conflicting updates in a controlled order. Assert that the first permitted write succeeds and the stale second precondition is rejected without lost data. For draft, separately test the exclusive-lock and total-ETag situations. A sequential test that rereads after every update never exercises a stale writer.
questions.detail: Alice and Ben read the same entity instance with its entity ETag. Alice updates that instance successfully; Ben submits an update to that same instance using the stale ETag and must not overwrite it. Separately test child-only active changes against the configured draft total ETag when resuming an expired draft lock. Keep entity-level conditional update and draft-resume concurrency assertions distinct.
questions.pitfall: Two updates in one shared transaction are not a realistic two-user concurrency test.
followups: How do you control the interleaving?
Which field protects the whole draft object?
questions.evidence: Capture request versions, responses and final values for the orchestrated conflicting sessions.

questions.question: Fiori still displays an old total after a successful action. How do you separate UI refresh from backend correctness?
questions.answer: Check the actual operation response and a fresh read of the authoritative BO state. If the backend value is wrong, inspect derivation triggers and transactional reads. If the backend is correct, inspect the action result, side-effect declarations, requested fields and consumer support. Avoid adding a second calculation in the UI that conceals missing backend consistency. Test the real deployed metadata rather than only a local preview.
questions.detail: Changing an item updates the server total but the header remains stale. Compare a direct read, a new UI session and the original session network requests. The correction may be a targeted refresh contract, not another commit or a full-page reload.
questions.pitfall: A page reload workaround does not explain whether the backend or refresh contract was defective.
followups: What does a fresh service read return?
Which request should refresh the affected property?
questions.evidence: Record action and follow-up reads with before/after values in the actual consumer.

references.title: SAP RAP side effects

questions.question: A RAP list becomes slow after enabling count and expanding children. What do you measure first?
questions.answer: Decompose the request into data selection, total count, expansion, authorization and any ABAP or remote enrichment. Use available traces and representative parameters to measure rows, calls, database time and application time. Optimize the observed bottleneck while preserving query and security semantics. Restrict unnecessary fields or expansions where the contract permits, and verify changes with the same workload rather than an unrelated microbenchmark.
questions.detail: A 20-row page triggers an expensive count across millions of authorized records plus child expansion. Removing a SELECT from one handler may be irrelevant. Compare page-only, count-only and expanded requests, including a restricted user whose authorization predicate changes the plan.
questions.pitfall: Do not optimize the shortest visible SELECT before finding the dominant request cost.
followups: Is count more expensive than the page?
What changes for an authorization-restricted user?
questions.evidence: Retain comparable request traces and latency/row/call measurements before and after the change.

questions.question: A custom entity calls a remote API once for every returned row. How would you remove the N+1 pattern?
questions.answer: Look for supported bulk reads, selective remote filters or bounded prefetch keyed by the requested result set. Consider a governed cache or read model only with explicit freshness and scope rules. Avoid fetching the whole remote dataset to save call overhead. Propagate partial and transient failures honestly, protect credentials and tenant boundaries, and define an upper bound on work per request.
questions.detail: One list page of 50 items makes 51 remote calls. A bulk endpoint can retrieve the needed reference data in one request, but may return partial failures. Test missing references, duplicate keys and service throttling, not only the happy-path call count.
questions.pitfall: An unbounded cache can trade latency for stale or cross-user data leakage.
followups: What is the maximum request size?
How are partial remote failures represented?
questions.evidence: Measure remote-call count and transferred rows while testing missing data and rate limits.

questions.question: A service works in development but fails after transport. What evidence should the handoff have included?
questions.answer: Separate transported repository artifacts from required configuration, communication setup, identities, roles, endpoint exposure and frontend deployment. Verify dependency order and the exact active source/version in the target. A published local service binding or preview in development does not establish a consumable production endpoint. The handoff should identify owners and verifiable readiness checks for each non-code dependency.
questions.detail: The behavior activates, but an outbound destination or communication arrangement is missing. Another issue is a target role not granting the service. Diagnose using the failure boundary and configuration evidence; do not change business code until the deployed source and configuration are reconciled.
questions.pitfall: A green transport import is not end-to-end service acceptance.
followups: Which required items are configuration rather than source?
Who verifies the real consuming identity?
questions.evidence: Use a target readiness checklist with actual endpoint, role, communication and smoke-test outcomes.

questions.question: How would you evolve a released RAP service when an action needs a new mandatory input?
questions.answer: Treat a new mandatory parameter as a potential breaking contract change. Assess existing consumers and choose a compatible optional/defaulted path only if its business meaning is valid; otherwise introduce a deliberate successor operation or version under the supported lifecycle. Keep old behavior operational during migration and provide deprecation guidance. Validate generated clients, metadata-driven UIs and non-UI consumers separately.
questions.detail: An approval action now requires a legal justification that old clients cannot supply. An empty default may violate the real business rule. Plan a transition with a measurable consumer migration target rather than silently accepting invalid data or breaking every caller at once.
questions.pitfall: Do not call a signature change compatible merely because the server activates.
followups: Is a default legally/business valid?
How do you know which consumers still use the old contract?
questions.evidence: Run old/new consumer contract tests and track observed usage before retiring the old operation.

questions.question: A remote approval succeeded, but the RAP caller timed out. How should an operator recover?
questions.answer: Treat the outcome as uncertain until reconciled using stable correlation. Do not blindly resubmit a non-idempotent business action. Identify which system owns each committed effect and use the documented status query, idempotency contract or compensation process. Preserve a durable recovery record and route unresolved cases to an owner. A local rollback cannot erase a remote commit.
questions.detail: The remote workflow created an approval instance, but its response was lost. A retry should find or reuse that instance rather than create another. Include a later duplicate callback and an approval referring to an outdated local version.
questions.pitfall: A timeout is not evidence that the other system performed no work.
followups: What is the stable correlation key?
Who resolves an outcome that cannot be queried?
questions.evidence: Simulate lost responses and verify one intended business effect plus a visible recoverable status.

questions.question: A failed save leaves no business record, but support still needs diagnostics. How would you log it safely?
questions.answer: Distinguish transactional business audit data from operational diagnostics and user-facing messages. Data written in the same rolled-back transaction may disappear, while independent commits from behavior code violate transaction ownership. Use supported logging/monitoring facilities with documented lifecycle and privacy behavior. Correlate failures without exposing secrets or persisting a false successful business event.
questions.detail: A validation rejects an order and REPORTED provides a user message. Support needs a correlation to an observed request failure. Decide what belongs in the service/application monitoring layer and what must be saved only alongside a successful business transition.
questions.pitfall: Do not add COMMIT WORK inside a handler just to preserve a log entry.
followups: Should this record survive a rollback?
Is it diagnostic evidence or a business audit event?
questions.evidence: Test success and rollback, then inspect which messages and logs survive through supported mechanisms.

questions.question: A production incident starts after a release. How do you contain it without making the data worse?
questions.answer: Establish affected scope, current version and the failing transaction boundary before changing code or replaying messages. Stop or limit the damaging path through authorized operational controls, preserve diagnostic evidence and assess already committed effects. Reconcile data and queues before choosing rollback, forward fix or controlled replay. A code rollback is not a general data rollback.
questions.detail: A new Submit action duplicates downstream approvals. Disable the affected scheduled initiation if authorized, retain correlations and identify duplicate effects. Repair idempotency and reconcile existing approvals before resuming a backlog, with a measured recovery window.
questions.pitfall: Do not rerun the whole backlog while the duplicate-creation defect remains active.
followups: What effects are already durable?
What proves it is safe to resume processing?
questions.evidence: Produce an incident timeline, affected-record reconciliation and a controlled post-fix replay result.

questions.question: What belongs in a RAP release gate beyond a passing ATC run?
questions.answer: Combine static findings with contract and behavior tests, relevant authorization cases, concurrency and rollback checks, representative performance evidence, dependency/API compatibility and target configuration readiness. Scale the gate to the changed risks. ATC can identify configured code issues but does not prove all business invariants or real integration behavior. Record unexecuted checks explicitly rather than converting missing evidence into a pass.
questions.detail: A change touches an action signature and an approval event. Required evidence differs from a label-only UI change: include old consumer compatibility, duplicate delivery and negative authorization. Tie each check to the relevant source revision and environment.
questions.pitfall: A universal checklist is not a substitute for checking the risks actually changed.
followups: Which new failure mode did this change introduce?
Which result is pending rather than passed?
questions.evidence: Present a concise release matrix linking changed behavior to executed results, owners and remaining risks.

questions.question: A team advertises 95% coverage while never asserting FAILED or persisted state. How would you improve it?
questions.answer: Treat coverage as a reachability signal, not proof of correct behavior. Identify critical invariants and failure modes, then add assertions that would fail if those rules were broken. Cover rejected operations, message identity, transactional cleanup and unintended side effects. Avoid adding dummy executable code or tests that merely mirror assignments. Use coverage to locate blind spots after meaningful test design.
questions.detail: A test executes a validation but never checks whether the invalid instance is rejected. Temporarily remove the rejection logic: if the test stays green, it does not prove the rule. Improve the assertion rather than increasing the number of similar happy-path calls.
questions.pitfall: High statement coverage can coexist with a broken business contract.
followups: Would the test fail if the rule were removed?
Which invariant is more important than the percentage?
questions.evidence: Demonstrate tests that fail for deliberately broken rejection or persistence behavior, then restore the implementation.

questions.question: How would you prepare an extension for a platform upgrade?
questions.answer: Inventory the actual used APIs, extension contracts, classifications and target-release changes. Prioritize critical business paths and known exceptions, then run focused regression and consumer tests in a representative target environment. Verify generated metadata, authorization, draft behavior, performance and required configuration where affected. A previously released API reduces a category of risk but does not remove the need to test your own assumptions and integration.
questions.detail: The extension uses a classic dependency behind a wrapper and a released service consumed externally. Give each a named owner and an upgrade test strategy. A deprecated successor path may require consumer migration before the old dependency can be retired.
questions.pitfall: Do not treat last year's clean ATC report as evidence for the new target release.
followups: Which dependencies drive the upgrade risk?
What behavior did your code assume beyond the documented contract?
questions.evidence: Record target versions, dependency classification and regression results for the highest-impact flows.

questions.question: A cloud job processes 500,000 records and times out. How would you redesign it?
questions.answer: Partition work into bounded, restartable units with stable business identities and checkpoints. Use supported background/application-job capabilities for the target environment rather than assuming classic task APIs are available. Control parallelism, database contention and remote limits. Define which units commit independently and how uncertain outcomes are reconciled. Progress reporting should distinguish processed, failed and pending items.
questions.detail: A pricing recalculation finishes the first 20 partitions before failure. A restart should skip safely completed work and detect conflicting newer updates. Test a crash between the business effect and checkpoint handling so the design does not rely on an unproven exactly-once assumption.
questions.pitfall: Moving a huge synchronous loop into a background job does not solve its transaction or restart design.
followups: What is one independently recoverable unit?
How do newer user edits interact with retry?
questions.evidence: Inject mid-partition failures and verify recovery, resource limits and final reconciliation.

references.title: SAP application job catalog and template
references.note: Read the supported job execution model, then design bounded units and restart checkpoints for the workload.

questions.question: How would you communicate senior readiness when you can review code locally but cannot run SAP checks?
questions.answer: Separate what was inspected, prepared and actually executed. A local source review can identify contract defects and propose tests, but cannot establish activation, real authorization, ATC results or measured SAP runtime behavior. Provide a precise target execution handoff with expected outcomes and dependencies. This is stronger evidence than inventing a pass or quoting performance numbers from a different environment.
questions.detail: For a RAP approval change, supply positive/negative EML cases, a two-session concurrency script, role prerequisites and a service smoke test. State the relevant source revision and what must be returned from the target before claiming acceptance.
questions.pitfall: Do not present prepared test code or a mocked UI as successful SAP integration.
followups: Which claim can you prove now?
What exact target result would close the remaining risk?
signals: Ties results to source and environment
questions.evidence: Provide a prepared/executed/pending matrix with specific acceptance criteria and accountable owners.
